page: Amazon Web Services m7i.large is a general-purpose instance belonging to the m7i server family. It features an x86_64 architecture powered by an Intel Xeon 8488C processor running at 3.2 GHz. The instance provides 2 vCPUs derived from 1 physical core with hyper-threading enabled. It is equipped with 8.0 GB of DDR5 memory operating at 5 GHz, translating to 4.0 GB of RAM per core. No local storage or GPUs are bundled with this instance, and the baseline network bandwidth is rated at 1 Gbps.

Benchmark data indicates a clear divergence between single-core and multi-core capabilities. The instance achieves average performance in single-core metrics, with a stress-ng single-core score of 1845.29 and a Geekbench single-core score of 1747.0. However, multi-core and memory-intensive operations show limitations. The stress-ng multi-core score of 1895.08 and the Geekbench multi-core score of 2133.0 are categorized as poor and weak respectively. Memory bandwidth tests also reflect lower-tier performance, with large block read-only bandwidth at 13.5 GB/sec and write bandwidth at 14.89 GB/sec.

Despite the lower multi-core and memory bandwidth scores, the processor supports advanced instruction sets including Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) and AVX-512, which assist in specialized workloads. For instance, LLM inference for prompt processing on a small 135M model reaches 306.2 tokens/sec. Given its 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM ratio and dedicated CPU allocation, this instance is suited for general-purpose workloads, basic text processing, and single-threaded applications that do not require high memory throughput or local storage.
description: Amazon Web Services m7i.large is a general-purpose instance featuring an Intel Xeon 8488C processor with 2 vCPUs, 1 physical core, and 8.0 GB of DDR5 memory. However, multi-core and memory-intensive benchmarks show notable constraints, with a multi-core Geekbench score of 2133.0 and a large-block read memory bandwidth of 13.5 GB/sec. Supported by Intel AMX and AVX-512 instruction sets, it is best suited for light general-purpose applications, single-threaded tasks, and basic text processing workloads where high multi-core density is not required.
